item.title: Python Iterators vs Generators Key Differences and Use Cases
item.description:
“Python Iterators vs Generators Key Differences and Use Cases”

What are the core distinctions between Python’s Iterator objects and Generator objects, and when should one favor implementing the full Iterator protocol over using the simpler yield keyword? How do these concepts relate to Iterables?

Core Definitions and Relationships

A foundational point often causing confusion is the hierarchical relationship:

  • Iterator: An object adhering to the Iterator Protocol, possessing both __iter__() (returning self) and __next__() (or next() in Python 2) methods. It supplies the next item in a sequence and raises StopIteration when exhausted.
  • Iterable: An object that can be looped over. It must implement the __iter__() method, which returns an iterator object. Built-in collections like lists, tuples, and strings are iterables.
  • Generator: A specialized, convenient form of an iterator created by calling a function that contains one or more yield expressions, or by using a generator expression. Every generator is an iterator, but not every iterator is a generator.

It is confirmed that issubclass(types.GeneratorType, collections.abc.Iterator) returns True, and issubclass(collections.abc.Iterator, collections.abc.Iterable) is also True.

item.title: Python Generators Explained: Key Concepts and Use Cases
item.description:
“Python Generators Explained: Key Concepts and Use Cases”

Generators in Python offer a distinct approach to creating iterators. Instead of returning a single value and ending, a generator function pauses its execution at a yield statement, preserving its internal state and returning a value. This allows for seamless resumption of the function’s execution from where it left off during subsequent calls. This mechanism is fundamentally different from regular functions, which always restart from the beginning and discard their state upon returning.
